CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying the outer function before the inner function.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Composition f(g(x)) is nested evaluation and order matters.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Evaluate g(x) first then feed its result to f.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Restoring a cancelled denominator zero to the quotient domain.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Track exclusions from the unsimplified quotient.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Checking the domain of only the inner function.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The output may be forbidden by the outer function.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Intersect the inner domain with g(x)∈D(f).

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming the two composition orders always agree.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Evaluate both orders and check their units and domains.

ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goals: combine function values by arithmetic, interpret composition as an ordered mapping, evaluate composite functions with tables, graphs and formulas, determine composite domains, and decompose a rule into inner and outer functions.
The quotient f/g requires x in the domains of both factors and g(x)≠0. Removing a symbolic factor cannot restore a forbidden input.
The composition (f∘g)(x) evaluates inner g then outer f, and generally differs from (g∘f)(x). The same procedure holds for chained tables and graphs: verify each intermediate input exists.
Composite domains depend on restrictions of g and on whether its outputs lie in the allowable input domain of f. Always test both layers.
Applied composition must have meaningful quantities and compatible units across the inner-output/outer-input interface.
A composite can be decomposed into two functions; multiple decompositions may exist, but they must reproduce the original formula and domain.

Edulytics independent cooldown: (a) Given f(x)=1/(x−2) and g(x)=x+1, find f(g(x)) and its domain. (b) Give a pair of simple functions for which f∘g and g∘f differ. (c) Explain why a quotient's removable factor does not restore the excluded input.
Independent Try It 1 — Operations and original quotient domain. With f(x)=x−2 and g(x)=x²−4, find (fg)(x), (f−g)(x), and their domains.
Independent Try It 2 — Unit-compatible composition. Let G(r) be gravitational force for orbital distance r and a(F) acceleration caused by force F. Form the physically meaningful composition.
Independent Try It 3 — Nested table lookups. Let f(1)=6,f(2)=5,f(3)=2,f(4)=7 and g(1)=3,g(2)=4,g(3)=1,g(4)=2. Find f(g(1)) and g(f(3)).
Independent Try It 4 — Graph composition with labelled points. An independent plot gives f(2)=4 and g(4)=1. Find g(f(2)).
Independent Try It 5 — Two numerical compositions. For f(x)=x²−2x and h(x)=2x+3, evaluate h(f(2)) and h(f(−2)).
Independent Try It 6 — Nested square root and reciprocal domain. Let f(x)=1/(x−3) and g(x)=√(x+2). Find domain of f(g(x)).
Independent Try It 7 — Construct inside and outside expressions. Decompose H(x)=4/(5−√(x²+2)) into an inner and outer function and state its domain.

KeyConcepts.Title: Function arithmetic
KeyConcepts.Definition: Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division combine output values pointwise.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The quotient domain is the common domain of f,g with g(x)≠0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Composition
KeyConcepts.Rule: Output of the inner function must belong to the outer function's domain.

KeyConcepts.Title: Composition order
KeyConcepts.Rule: Even when both exist, inner/outer meaning and units determine the valid order.
KeyConcepts.Example: d(hours) gives miles and u(miles) gives gallons, so u(d(hours)).

KeyConcepts.Title: Table and graph composition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Follow the first mapping to an intermediate value, then apply the second mapping.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A missing intermediate table input makes that composition undefined.
KeyConcepts.Example: If g(1)=2 and f(2)=5, then f(g(1))=5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Composite domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: The allowed x-values are in the inner domain and map to allowed inputs of the outer function.
KeyConcepts.Example: If f(u)=1/(u−2) and g(x)=√x, exclude x<0 and x=4.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decomposition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A complicated formula can be expressed as outer rule evaluated on inner rule.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Different valid choices for components can yield the same composite.

SummaryPoints: Arithmetic on functions is pointwise and division excludes denominator zeros.
(f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)) applies the inner function first; changing order may change meaning.
For table/graph composition each intermediate output must be a valid next input.
A composite domain restricts both the inner rule and the outer rule's accepted inputs.
Contextual unit compatibility helps identify meaningful composition order.
First-party open-ended source skills are teacher-reviewed in Stage C.
Lessons.Title: Composition of Functions

Visuals.Title: First-party composition lookup table
Visuals.Description: Use the output of g as a valid input of f; reverse order yields different outputs.

Visuals.Title: Domain restriction for nested operations
Visuals.Description: Different source-skill restrictions arise from inner and outer formula domains.

WorkedExamples.Title: Different algebraic operations on functions
WorkedExamples.Question: Let f(x)=x−2 and g(x)=x²−4. Find (g−f)(x) and (g/f)(x), including their original domains.
WorkedExamples.Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Steps: Although the quotient simplifies, the original divisor vanishes at x=2.
WorkedExamples.Answer: (g−f)(x)=x²−x−2 for all real x; (g/f)(x)=x+2 for x≠2.
WorkedExamples.Check: Removing a factor cannot restore an excluded input.

WorkedExamples.Title: Composition order need not commute
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=3x+2 and g(x)=4−x, compare f(g(x)) and g(f(x)).
WorkedExamples.Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Steps: The outputs differ by 12 at every x.
WorkedExamples.Check: Changing order changes meaning even when both domains are ℝ.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret a composite contextual output
WorkedExamples.Question: Let s(t) count steps walked by time t (minutes); let c(s) be estimated kilocalories expended after s steps. Interpret c(s(5)).
WorkedExamples.Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Steps: The inner function s(5) converts five minutes into step count.
That step count is a valid input to outer c.
The composite output is kilocalories expended from the steps walked during the first five minutes.
WorkedExamples.Answer: c(s(5)) describes estimated energy expended (kilocalories) from a five-minute walk.
WorkedExamples.Check: The output and input units at the function boundary must agree.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose a meaningful function order
WorkedExamples.Question: Let d(h) map travel hours to miles driven; let u(m) map miles driven to gallons used. Which expression predicts gallons after h hours?
WorkedExamples.Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Steps: Feed the result as the miles input to u.
The reverse composition d(u(m)) treats gallons as hours and is physically mismatched.
WorkedExamples.Answer: u(d(h)) with units gallons; the reverse composition lacks the declared interface.
WorkedExamples.Check: Physical units validate meaningful composition order.

WorkedExamples.Title: Nested lookup from two tables
WorkedExamples.Question: Let f(1)=5, f(2)=4, f(3)=1 and g(1)=3, g(2)=1, g(3)=2. Evaluate f(g(1)) and g(f(3)).
WorkedExamples.Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Steps: Every intermediate value must be in the input domain of the next table.

WorkedExamples.Title: Composition from graph coordinates
WorkedExamples.Question: Independent graphs show g(1)=2 and f(2)=5. Find f(g(1)), explaining how two graph readings are combined.
WorkedExamples.Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Steps: Start on the g graph at x=1 to obtain output 2.
Use 2 as the x-input on the f graph and read output 5.
WorkedExamples.Check: Read actual plotted coordinates, not the original input twice.

WorkedExamples.Title: Nested formula numeric evaluation
WorkedExamples.Question: Let f(t)=t²−2t and h(x)=2x+3. Evaluate f(h(2)) and h(f(2)).
WorkedExamples.Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
WorkedExamples.Check: The inner function must be evaluated before the outer function.

WorkedExamples.Title: Domain of nested quotient functions
WorkedExamples.Question: Let f(x)=6/(x−2) and g(x)=3/(x−1). Find domain of f(g(x)).
WorkedExamples.Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Steps: 3/(x−1)=2 implies x=5/2; exclude this additional input.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both restrictions are required even after algebraic simplification.

WorkedExamples.Title: Decomposition into inner and outer maps
WorkedExamples.Question: Write H(x)=√(7−x²) as a composition using independent functions.
WorkedExamples.Method: Perform the inner function first for composition; preserve the domain of every original operation.
Steps: Then H=b∘a and its real domain requires 7−x²≥0.
WorkedExamples.Check: Composition can be decomposed in more than one mathematically valid way.
